title: Plant transport: follow the water and sugar
subtitle: Trace two transport systems, then investigate a water-uptake proxy
objective: Explain plant transport and use potometer evidence to infer how air movement affects water uptake.

sow.alignment: Directly develops C37 and Pearson 6.7–6.10,6.12–6.13. Core routes explain transport and simple rate calculations; optional volume calculation extends mathematical demand without assuming Higher-tier entry.

priorLearning: Photosynthesis makes glucose using light energy.
Water can move across partially permeable membranes by osmosis.
Rate is change divided by time.
success: Distinguish xylem water/mineral transport from phloem sucrose transport.
Explain evaporation and diffusion of water vapour at a leaf.
Calculate a potometer rate and explain why uptake is a proxy for transpiration.

vocabulary.meaning: Transport tissue with hollow, lignified dead conducting cells carrying water and mineral ions.
Living transport tissue that moves dissolved sucrose between sources and sinks.
Loss of water vapour from aerial plant parts, mainly through leaf stomata.
Transport of dissolved organic substances such as sucrose in phloem.
A pore in the leaf surface, controlled by guard cells.
Apparatus that measures water uptake by a shoot; uptake can indicate transpiration.

equipment: Printed shared evidence and one selected response route; pen, ruler and calculator.
Projector or offline HTML/PowerPoint. Optional word processor or spreadsheet.
Optional prepared demonstration: school-approved potometer with leafy shoot, stable support, timer, ruler, thermometer and cool fan. Complete paper route requires none of these.
preparation: Print the shared evidence page, one chosen response route and exit page. Routes are alternatives, not a workload ladder.
Read the teacher answers before teaching. All numerical sample data in this lesson are constructed for learning.
If demonstrating, teacher/technician assembles and leak-tests the apparatus; cuts and inserts the shoot under water to avoid air entering the xylem. Pupils do not force stems into glass tubing.

Compare the same shoot and capillary over equal intervals; allow adjustment after changing conditions. Monitor temperature/light and keep them comparable. Repeat conditions and record actual results separately.
safety: Default task is paper/data analysis. Optional potometer must be prepared and checked by teacher/technician.
Adults handle sharp cutting and fragile glass. Secure the apparatus, keep water away from electrical equipment and use a stable cool fan.
No tasting plant material; wash hands after handling. Use a plant approved for school handling and avoid known irritants.
practicalAlternative: Use the supplied diagram, repeated movement table and source cards. Draw arrows and calculate the same rates without assembling a potometer.

misconceptions.claim: Xylem carries plant food from the roots.
misconceptions.correction: Xylem carries water and mineral ions; photosynthesis makes organic material and phloem moves sucrose.
misconceptions.check: Ask which material came from photosynthesis.

misconceptions.correction: Sucrose moves from a source to a sink; different tubes can carry it in different directions.
misconceptions.check: Point to a growing bud above a source leaf and roots below it.

misconceptions.claim: Liquid water simply escapes as liquid through stomata.
misconceptions.correction: Water evaporates from internal cell surfaces; water vapour diffuses through stomata.
misconceptions.check: Ask pupils to name the state change and then the movement process.

misconceptions.correction: Much absorbed water replaces transpiration loss, but some is used or retained; leaks and storage changes also affect readings.
misconceptions.check: Ask what quantity the bubble movement measures directly.

access.supported: Same core scientific goal, with word bank, short prompts, read-aloud or pointing/dictation. Do not assign a route from diagnosis.
access.standard: Use the supplied evidence to explain and justify an independent scientific decision.
access.stretch: Optional challenge after secure core: evaluate a limitation and transfer the science. Higher-tier-only material, where present, is labelled explicitly.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence. Offer solo or partner work, a pass and quiet response. Allow a brief reset and re-entry at the next numbered task; no compulsory disclosure, performance or speed competition.

slides.title: How does water reach a leaf?
body: Mission: trace materials, then test a transport explanation.
A moving bubble is evidence—but evidence of what?
slides.notes: Invite prediction; no need to know transpiration term yet. Show the planned distinction between material transport and a measurement of uptake.

slides.title: What moves and why?
body: R1. What useful sugar does photosynthesis first make?
R2. Name the process by which water crosses a partially permeable membrane.
R3. How do you calculate a rate?
slides.notes: R1 glucose. R2 osmosis. R3 change/amount divided by time. Explain glucose can be converted to sucrose for transport; root uptake is not sugar absorption from soil.

slides.title: I follow one material at a time
body: Xylem carries water and mineral ions.
Phloem transports dissolved sucrose from source to sink.
Different tubes can carry sucrose in different directions.
slides.notes: Model blue path from roots to leaf. Root hairs give large area; water can enter by osmosis, while mineral ions may require active transport. Then model leaf-to-bud and leaf-to-root sucrose paths. Xylem conducting cells are hollow/dead with lignified walls; phloem includes living cells and energy-dependent loading/transport processes.

visual.title: Two tissues, different jobs
visual.description: Whole-plant transport model: blue xylem arrows carry water and mineral ions from roots towards the leaves. Purple phloem paths move sucrose from a source leaf to a growing bud above and roots below in different tubes. Plant and paths are schematic, not to scale.

slides.title: The leaf links water loss to transport
body: Water evaporates from internal moist surfaces.
Water vapour diffuses through stomata.
This loss helps draw water through xylem.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “First liquid becomes vapour: evaporation. Then vapour spreads out through the pore: diffusion. I should not call these the same process.” Wind can remove humid air near the leaf, increasing the vapour gradient if other conditions are comparable.

visual.description: Leaf-section model: water at moist internal cell surfaces evaporates into internal air spaces. Water vapour diffuses through a stoma to the air when a gradient exists. Guard cells control the pore. Shapes are schematic, not a complete leaf section.

slides.title: I name the measured quantity
body: Bubble distance ÷ time gives movement rate.
Worked example:15 mm ÷5 min =3 mm/min.
Water uptake is a proxy for transpiration.
slides.notes: Trace the bubble towards shoot. “This is movement along a capillary, not water vapour counted at a leaf. Most uptake may replace loss, but some water is used/retained; leaks matter.” Equal tubing permits comparative movement rates; volume requires cross-sectional area.

visual.title: A moving bubble indicates water uptake
visual.description: Schematic bubble potometer: the shoot takes up water, drawing an air bubble along the graduated capillary towards the shoot. The measured distance over time indicates volume uptake only when capillary cross-section is known. It is not a direct measurement of water vapour loss.

slides.title: Air-movement investigation
body: W1. Find the mean movement in each condition.
Divide by 5 minutes to compare rates.
slides.notes: Still mean 12 mm; moving mean 30 mm. Rates 2.4 and 6 mm/min. Constructed matched shoot/light/temperature/capillary data; effects are conditional, not a universal fixed wind multiplier.

slides.title: Trace the explanation backwards
body: W2. Moving air gave faster uptake here.
Explain from surrounding air → leaf loss → xylem uptake.
slides.notes: Moving air removes humid air near stomata, increasing diffusion gradient; more water evaporates/is lost; uptake through xylem tends to replace it. No claim fan pushes water through leaf. Accept accurate arrow chain.

slides.title: Repair the instrument claim
body: W3. “The bubble proves exactly how much water evaporated.”
What should the label say instead?
slides.notes: “Water-uptake proxy” or “bubble movement indicating uptake.” Uptake may differ from loss; volume not directly known from distance alone. Ask what extra quantity converts distance to volume: cross-sectional area.
slides.reveal: Measure bubble movement per time. Infer water uptake; treat transpiration as a proxy relationship.

slides.title: Choose the accurate transport statement
body: Read the material and direction carefully.
slides.notes: B correct. A swaps tissue/material; C swaps measurement/inference; D misses source/sink.

options.text: Xylem carries sucrose made in the roots.
options.feedback: Xylem carries water/mineral ions; phloem transports sucrose between sources and sinks.

options.text: Water evaporates inside a leaf and vapour diffuses through stomata.
options.feedback: Yes: state change first, then diffusion through the pore.

options.text: A potometer directly measures all water vapour leaving a leaf.
options.feedback: A bubble potometer measures uptake; it does not collect all vapour loss.
A sink may be above or below a source; different tubes can transport in different directions.

slides.title: Prepare the transport report
body: Choose your route.
Show a material path, a rate and a justified limit.
slides.notes: Shared evidence supplied. Let pupils point or narrate arrows rather than require lengthy prose.

slides.title: Make the explanation traceable
body: Material → tissue → destination.
Movement → calculation → inference → limitation.
slides.notes: Supported S1–S4; standard M1–M4; stretch T1–T4. Check that moving air explanation includes vapour gradient, not fan pushing liquid. If numbers confuse, model rate from a 10 mm/5 min example.

slides.title: Audience: follow my arrows
body: L1. Show one material route or measurement.
Audience asks: “Is that measured or inferred?”
slides.notes: Quiet partner/TA review. Pupil adds tissue label or changes “exact transpiration” to an accurate uptake label.

slides.title: A careful transport explanation
body: The tissue explains the path.
The leaf explains the loss.
The apparatus defines the measurement.
slides.notes: Model still 2.4 versus moving 6 mm/min in the supplied setup; stronger air movement is consistent with faster uptake, not a direct measurement of every evaporated molecule.

slides.title: Name the path and the proxy
body: E1. Name the tissue carrying sucrose.
E2. 20 mm in 5 minutes: calculate movement rate.
E3. Why is uptake not exact transpiration?
slides.notes: E1 phloem. E2=4 mm/min. E3 some water used/retained and apparatus limitations. Collect one precise response.

slides.title: Choose the next useful step
body: Tissue roles • leaf mechanism • rate • proxy.
slides.notes: Shared exit minute. Revisit a source leaf with sinks above/below if downward-only misconception persists.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence | Plant transport and air movement
pupilPages.intro: Constructed potometer data: same shoot, capillary, light and 20°C. Each value is bubble movement over 5 minutes after adjustment.

cards.title: Roots and xylem
cards.text: Root hairs provide a large surface. Water can enter by osmosis; mineral ions may require active transport. Hollow, lignified xylem conducting cells carry water and mineral ions.

cards.title: Phloem
cards.text: Living tissue moves dissolved sucrose from source to sink. A source leaf may supply roots below and a growing bud above using different tubes.

cards.title: Leaf and air
cards.text: Water evaporates from moist internal surfaces. Vapour diffuses through stomata. Moving air may remove humid air around the leaf.

cards.title: Potometer limit
cards.text: Bubble movement indicates water uptake. Some water is used or retained; leaks can affect readings. Uptake does not exactly equal transpiration.

blocks.prompt: W1. Calculate rates. W2. Explain the air effect. W3. Correct the exact-evaporation claim.

pupilPages.title: Supported route | Trace and calculate
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: water/mineral ions; sucrose; xylem; phloem; evaporation; diffusion; uptake.

blocks.prompt: S1. Draw two labelled arrows: roots→leaf for water/mineral ions, and leaf→a sink for sucrose. Name each tissue.
S2. Describe evaporation inside the leaf and diffusion out of the stoma.
S3. Calculate the mean movement and rate for still and moving air.
S4. Explain why the faster bubble is evidence about uptake, not an exact transpiration measurement.

pupilPages.title: Standard route | Write the transport report
pupilPages.intro: Use the source cards and repeat table.

blocks.prompt: M1. Compare xylem and phloem by transported material, cell structure and direction/source-to-sink role.
M2. Explain how water moves from root to surrounding air, including osmosis, xylem, evaporation and diffusion.
M3. Calculate both mean movements and rates. Describe the difference using units.
M4. Explain the air-movement result and give two requirements for a fair, valid comparison.

pupilPages.title: Stretch route | From distance to volume
pupilPages.intro: Optional calculation. For this constructed capillary, cross-sectional area=0.5 mm². Volume=area×distance. Use the shared mean movements.

blocks.prompt: T1. Calculate mean water-uptake volume and volume per minute in both conditions. Give mm³ and mm³/min.
T2. Why would comparing distance rates in tubes with different diameters be misleading?
T3. A shoot wilts and its stomata close during a stronger fan trial. Must uptake keep rising? Explain a competing effect.
T4. Propose a check for an apparatus error and a separate improvement to the biological comparison.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection | Follow the material

blocks.prompt: E1. What tissue carries sucrose from source to sink?
E2. Calculate 20 mm in 5 minutes, with a unit.
E3. Give one reason uptake need not equal exact transpiration.
L1. What did your audience question? Improve one arrow, label or claim.

answers.label: Retrieval
answers.answer: R1 glucose, which can be converted to sucrose for transport. R2 osmosis. R3 change/amount divided by time.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1 means 12 mm and 30 mm; rates 12/5=2.4 mm/min and 30/5=6 mm/min. W2 moving air can remove humid air, increasing the vapour gradient and loss; xylem uptake tends to replace that loss. W3 bubble movement indicates uptake, not exact evaporation; distance alone also lacks volume unless area is known.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: A false: xylem/materials reversed. B correct: evaporation then diffusion. C false: uptake measurement is a transpiration proxy. D false: phloem transports source-to-sink, which can be up or down in different tubes.

answers.label: S1 / M1
answers.answer: Xylem: water/mineral ions, hollow dead conducting cells with lignified walls, mainly root-to-leaf stream. Phloem: living cells, dissolved sucrose from sources to sinks; different tubes can serve sinks above/below. Energy is involved in phloem transport processes.

answers.label: S2 / M2
answers.answer: Water enters root cells by osmosis and moves through root tissues into xylem. Water is drawn along xylem towards leaves; it evaporates from moist internal surfaces and water vapour diffuses through stomata. Root hairs increase uptake area; mineral-ion uptake may require active transport.

answers.label: S3 / M3
answers.answer: Still mean(12+11+13)/3=12 mm; moving mean(30+28+32)/3=30 mm. Divide each by 5 minutes:2.4 and 6 mm/min. Difference 3.6 mm/min; moving value 2.5 times still in this constructed setup.

answers.label: S4
answers.answer: The bubble tracks water entering the shoot. Some water is used in processes or retained, and water stores can change; leaks affect readings. Thus uptake and loss are related but not exactly identical.

answers.label: M4
answers.answer: Moving air can remove humid air near stomata and increase the diffusion gradient, promoting water loss and replacement uptake. Same shoot/leaf area, capillary, light, temperature and time; allow adjustment, repeat, and check seal/leaks. Any two justified controls/checks earn the method element.

answers.label: T1
answers.answer: Still:0.5×12=6 mm³ over 5 minutes;6/5=1.2 mm³/min. Moving:0.5×30=15 mm³;15/5=3 mm³/min. Units must distinguish volume from distance.

answers.label: T2
answers.answer: The same distance represents different volumes when cross-sectional areas differ. Compare volume per time or use the same capillary; do not treat mm/min as universally comparable uptake.

answers.label: T3
answers.answer: No. Strong water stress can close stomata, reducing the diffusion pathway and water loss. Environmental effects depend on plant response; the original moderate-condition trend is not unlimited.

answers.label: T4
answers.answer: Apparatus: inspect/verify an airtight seal or test for leaks with an appropriate prepared setup. Biology: repeat with matched shoots/leaf areas or repeat condition order while controlling temperature/light. Accept an explicit check that targets an identified source of uncertainty.

answers.label: Exit and assessment
answers.answer: E1 phloem. E2 20/5=4 mm/min. E3 water used/retained or stores changing; a relevant apparatus limit also shows caution. L1 accepts a specific improvement or justified confirmation. Secure core includes correct tissue/material, evaporation/diffusion distinction and proxy-aware rate interpretation.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2, retrieval 3, I do 10, We do 7, hinge 3, independent 11, review 3, exit 1. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Choose one response route. Accept accurate speech, pointing plus explanation, annotations or writing as evidence.
A quiet review still has an audience: teacher or TA reads the pupil’s decision, asks one evidence question, and the pupil revises or confirms it.

The phloem diagram shows different transport paths; it does not claim simultaneous opposite bulk flow in one sieve tube. Keep source and sink tied to organ roles, which can change over a plant’s life.

Interactive We do predicts the effect of moderate moving air in the exact constructed table, tests the calculated rates, then checks the uptake/transpiration distinction. Paper W1–W3 uses the same values. Animated bubble motion is controlled and represents a measurement model, not a real plant simulation.
